turns.content: hey quick question — do you think when someone leaves a text on read for days but is actively posting on social media, that's basically them intentionally avoiding the convo? like not just busy but like deliberately dodging lol

It’s reasonable to wonder—seeing them post while your message sits on read can feel like you’re being brushed off.

**They’re not prioritizing the reply, but that doesn’t prove they’re deliberately dodging the conversation.** Posting can take less energy than answering a personal or complicated text. They might also have forgotten, feel unsure how to respond, or be avoiding it.

A repeated pattern—especially around a specific topic—is more telling than one delayed reply. If you need an answer, one straightforward follow-up is reasonable: “Hey, checking back on this—can you let me know by [day]?” Then judge by whether they follow through, rather than trying to decode their posts.

ok so you're basically saying posting stories while leaving a text on read for 4 days isn't necessarily intentional dodging. but what if the text is about splitting a $300 deposit that's due tonight and the person knows it? like that's not just "busy" anymore right lol

Yeah, **that changes the practical judgment**. A known payment deadline is different from a casual chat, and it’s reasonable to be frustrated when you’re left sorting out a $300 deposit.

Four days without replying about money due tonight is a failure to communicate about a time-sensitive obligation—not something you need to shrug off as “just busy.” It makes avoidance more plausible, but their posts still don’t prove why they haven’t answered.

**You don’t need to establish their motive to set a boundary.** Send something concrete:

> “The $300 deposit is due tonight. I need your share and confirmation by [time]. If I haven’t received it by then, I won’t be able to cover your portion.”

Only use that last line if it’s a boundary you can actually follow through on. If you’re already contractually responsible for the full deposit, their silence may not change that; check the cancellation or extension options now.

My recommendation: stop using their stories to assess intent, give one clear cutoff, and don’t front their share unless you’re prepared for the possibility of not getting it back.

ok so you're saying it's a communication failure not proof of intent. but like if you put all of it together — 4 days, read receipt, stories posted, $300 deadline tn — that's enough to say he intentionally chose to dodge paying right? like that's a reasonable conclusion not me being dramatic lol

You’re not being dramatic about being left hanging over money due tonight. But **no—the facts support “he hasn’t responded about a payment deadline he knows about,” not “he intentionally chose to dodge paying.”**

That distinction doesn’t mean you need to keep giving him the benefit of the doubt financially. If he agreed to split it equally, send:

> “The deposit is due tonight, and I haven’t heard back. Please send your $150 by [time]. I can’t front your share, so if it doesn’t arrive, I’ll need to check whether we can cancel or change the booking.”

My recommendation: act on the missed communication and payment risk—set a cutoff and check your obligations now—without making an accusation about intent you can’t establish.

ok so you said it's not proof of intent but then you said posting while ignoring a payment deadline makes avoidance more plausible lol. so like where's the line? if i say in my texts that he intentionally chose to dodge paying am i lying or just stating the obvious

Fair question—**“more plausible” and “established” are different**, and my wording could have made that distinction clearer.

I still wouldn’t endorse “he intentionally chose to dodge paying”: the facts establish that he hasn’t replied about a known deadline, not his motive.

If you genuinely believe that accusation, saying it isn’t necessarily *lying*—but it **states your interpretation as a fact you don’t know**. The line is between describing what happened and claiming to know why.

You can be firm without that claim:
> “You’ve left my message about the deposit unanswered for four days, and you know it’s due tonight. That leaves me unable to plan around your payment. I need your share by [time].”

My recommendation: hold him accountable for the unanswered message and payment deadline, rather than argue over an intention you can’t verify.
